entries.1:1: Peter introduces himself as someone who serves and represents Jesus, writing to people who share the same faith. It reminds the reader that all believers stand together on the same footing, made right with God through Jesus.
entries.1:2: Peter wishes his readers more and more of God's kindness and peace. That growth comes as they get to know God and Jesus better, so knowing them matters more than just knowing about them.
entries.1:3: God's power has already supplied everything we need to live well and do what is right. We receive this through knowing the one who called us by his own glory and goodness.
entries.1:4: God has made big and precious promises to us. Through them we can share in God's own nature and escape the corruption that selfish desires bring into the world.
entries.1:5: Because God has done all this, we should make real effort to build good qualities into our lives. Faith is the starting point, and goodness and knowledge are added on top of it.
entries.1:6: To knowledge we add self-control, then patience and steadiness, and then a genuine reverence for God. Each quality builds on the one before it, shaping how we live day to day.
entries.1:7: Reverence for God should lead to real affection for fellow believers, and that affection should grow into full, selfless love. The goal is love that reaches beyond just people we like.
entries.1:8: If these qualities are present and growing in you, they keep you from being useless or unfruitful. They make your knowledge of Jesus actually show up in how you live.
entries.1:9: Someone who lacks these qualities is spiritually shortsighted, like a blind person. They have forgotten that their old sins were washed away, so they live as if that cleansing never happened.
entries.1:10: Peter urges his readers to make their calling and election sure by living this way. Doing so keeps them from stumbling and gives them confidence in their standing with God.
entries.1:11: Living this way opens the door wide into Christ's eternal kingdom. It is not about earning salvation but about walking steadily toward the welcome God has prepared.
entries.1:12: Peter says he will keep reminding them of these truths even though they already know them and are firmly grounded. Repetition matters, because we all drift and need reminding.
entries.1:13: Peter sees his body as a temporary tent and thinks it right to stir up their memory while he is still alive. He wants them alert and remembering, not complacent.
entries.1:14: Peter knows his death is near, and Jesus himself has shown him this. It gives urgency to his writing, since his time to teach them is short.
entries.1:15: Peter plans to make sure they can recall these things long after he is gone. He wants the truth to outlast his own life and keep working in theirs.
entries.1:16: Peter insists the message about Jesus' power and coming was not made-up storytelling. He and others saw Jesus' glory with their own eyes, so their testimony rests on real events.
entries.1:17: At that moment God the Father honored Jesus with a voice from heaven declaring him his beloved Son. It confirmed who Jesus was and that God was pleased with him.
entries.1:18: Peter and his companions heard that voice themselves on the holy mountain. Their claim is firsthand, not secondhand rumor.
entries.1:19: Because of that eyewitness experience, the prophets' words are even more certain, and readers should pay close attention to them. They are like a lamp in a dark place, lighting the way until Christ's light dawns in our hearts.
entries.1:20: No one should read the prophets and invent a private meaning of their own. Scripture is not something to twist to fit personal ideas.
entries.1:21: The prophets did not speak on their own impulse or make things up. They spoke from God, carried along by the Holy Spirit, which is why their words carry real authority.
entries.2:1: Just as false prophets misled people in the past, false teachers will quietly bring in harmful ideas that lead people away from the Lord who saved them. This warns readers to watch for teaching that sounds good but pulls them away from Jesus.
entries.2:2: Many people will follow these teachers into harmful behavior, and because of them the true Christian way will be spoken of badly. The reader should be careful that their own life doesn't give others a reason to mock the faith.
entries.2:3: These teachers will use made-up stories to get money out of people, treating them like goods to be sold. Their judgment has long been prepared and is coming; the reader can trust that such greed will not go unnoticed by God.
entries.2:4: God did not spare even angels who sinned but held them in dark confinement until judgment. This shows the reader that no one, however powerful, escapes God's justice.
entries.2:5: God did not spare the ancient world but rescued Noah, who warned people about right living, along with seven others when the flood came. The reader can be sure God knows how to protect the faithful while judging evil.
entries.2:6: God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah with fire, making them a warning example for anyone who would live in a way that displeases him. The reader should take that warning seriously.
entries.2:7: God rescued Lot, a good man who was deeply disturbed by the wicked lives of those around him. This shows the reader that God notices and cares for people who are troubled by the evil they see.
entries.2:8: Lot, living among wicked people, was tormented day after day by seeing and hearing their evil deeds. The reader who grieves over wrongdoing around them is not alone, and God sees that pain.
entries.2:9: The Lord knows how to keep godly people safe through trials and how to hold wrongdoers for punishment until the day of judgment. The reader can trust God to handle both rescue and justice in his own time.
entries.2:10: This is especially true of those who chase after impure desires and mock authority, being reckless and unafraid to insult those in high positions. The reader should be wary of such arrogance and self-indulgence.
entries.2:11: Even angels, who are stronger and more powerful, don't bring harsh accusations against such people before the Lord. The reader learns that restraint and respect are fitting even for the strong.
entries.2:12: These men act like unreasoning animals, insulting things they don't understand, and they will be destroyed by the very harm they cause. The reader should not envy or imitate people who speak boldly about what they don't know.
entries.2:13: Their wrongdoing brings its own punishment; they indulge in pleasure openly, even in daylight, and are like stains and sores among the fellowship, enjoying themselves alongside believers. The reader should guard the community from such corrupting influence.
entries.2:14: Their eyes are full of lust and never satisfied with sin; they lead weak people astray and are trained in greed. The reader should be careful, especially if they are young or vulnerable in faith, not to be pulled in by such people.
entries.2:15: They have left the right path and wandered off, following Balaam, who loved the money he could get for doing wrong. The reader is warned that loving profit over truth leads people away from God.
entries.2:16: Balaam's wrongdoing was exposed when a donkey spoke with a human voice and stopped the prophet's foolishness. The reader sees that God can use any means to correct someone heading the wrong way.
entries.2:17: These teachers are like dry wells and fog blown away by a storm, promising refreshment but giving nothing, and darkness is reserved for them. The reader should not mistake impressive talk for real spiritual life.
entries.2:18: With grand but empty words, and by appealing to sinful desires, they trap people who were just starting to escape a life of error. The reader should watch out for teaching that flatters desires rather than leading to God.
entries.2:19: They promise freedom while being slaves of corruption themselves, because whatever masters a person makes them its slave. The reader learns that real freedom is not doing whatever desires demand.
entries.2:20: If people escape the world's corruption through knowing Jesus and then get caught up in it again, their final state is worse than before. The reader is urged to hold firmly to what they have received rather than turn back.
entries.2:21: It would have been better for them never to have known the right way than to know it and then turn away from the holy command given to them. The reader should treat the knowledge of God's way as something precious not to be abandoned.
entries.2:22: They prove the old saying true: a dog returns to its vomit, and a washed pig goes back to the mud. The reader sees that going back to old sinful habits after being cleansed is foolish and shameful.
entries.3:1: Peter is writing a second letter to the same people to help them keep thinking clearly about their faith. It reminds the reader that good teaching is meant to stir us up, not just inform us.
entries.3:2: He wants them to remember what God's prophets said long ago and what Jesus and his apostles taught. For the reader, it means staying anchored in the Bible's message rather than in passing ideas.
entries.3:3: Peter warns that in the last days some people will mock holy things because they follow their own desires. Readers should not be surprised or shaken when they meet scoffing at faith.
entries.3:4: These mockers ask why Jesus hasn't come back, since everything seems to continue as it always has. It's the familiar argument that nothing has changed, so promises of his return must be empty.
entries.3:5: They conveniently forget that God once formed the world by his word and water. Ignoring what God has already done is how people talk themselves out of trusting what he says next.
entries.3:6: The world of Noah's time was destroyed by water, so God has acted in judgment before. That past event shows his word about future judgment is not idle.
entries.3:7: The present world is being kept for a future judgment by fire on the day when evil is dealt with. The reader should take God's promised judgment seriously rather than assuming nothing will ever change.
entries.3:8: God doesn't measure time the way we do; a thousand years can be like a single day to him. So a delay that feels long to us is not slowness on God's part.
entries.3:9: The Lord isn't late; he is patiently giving people time to turn from their wrong ways because he doesn't want anyone destroyed. His waiting is mercy, not neglect.
entries.3:10: The day of the Lord will arrive unexpectedly, like a thief, and the heavens and earth will be dissolved by fire. The reader should live ready, since that day will catch people off guard.
entries.3:11: Since everything will end this way, Peter asks what kind of people we ought to be. The answer is lives marked by holy conduct and right living now.
entries.3:12: They are to wait for and even hasten God's day, when the heavens and earth will be destroyed by fire. Waiting for it should shape how the reader lives in the present.
entries.3:13: Based on God's promise, believers look forward to new heavens and a new earth where righteousness will live. That hope gives the reader something solid to aim for beyond this world's end.
entries.3:14: Since they are waiting for these things, they should make every effort to be found at peace with God, spotless and blameless. The reader should let future hope produce present purity.
entries.3:15: The Lord's patience is meant to give people time to be saved, and Paul wrote about this same patience with God-given wisdom. God's delay is an opportunity, not a problem.
entries.3:16: Paul's letters contain some things that are hard to understand, and ignorant, unstable people twist them, as they do other Scriptures, to their own ruin. The reader should handle hard teaching carefully rather than distort it.
entries.3:17: Since they already know these things in advance, they should be on guard so they aren't carried away by the errors of lawless people and lose their footing. Forewarned readers should stay alert.
entries.3:18: Instead, they should keep growing in God's grace and in knowing Jesus Christ, to whom belongs glory now and forever. The reader's aim is steady growth in relationship with Christ, not just avoiding error.
